query: Earlier empirical-potential and first-principles studies primarily targeted phase-transition temperature, while other fusion properties remain difficult because they require free energies on both sides of the transition with vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron–vibration coupling retained. Explicit ab initio free-energy evaluation is highly accurate but depends on costly molecular dynamics. TOR-TILD increased throughput for elemental and binary systems, yet slows substantially for multicomponent high-entropy systems. Under the constraint that the free energies of both solid and fluid states and the relevant entropy terms remain faithful, what single testable methodological hypothesis could substantially reduce the cost of obtaining fusion and high-temperature thermodynamic properties? State the proposed intervention and why it should work, predict its speed and fidelity relative to explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics workflows and TOR-TILD, define composition and temperature boundaries, cite supporting evidence from prior elemental or binary results, and specify a decisive benchmark of phase free energies and derived observables that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Integrating machine‐learning trained interatomic potentials with quasi‐harmonic (and minimal anharmonic/correction) treatments can compute the free energies of both solid and fluid states at high temperatures with fidelity comparable to full ab initio MD but at a substantially reduced computational cost.
generation.material_initial_state: Elemental and binary metal systems (and ultimately multicomponent high‐entropy alloys) at temperatures approaching fusion, with full DFT-level treatment of vibrational and electronic entropy in both solid and liquid states.
generation.intervention: Replace full explicit ab initio MD free-energy evaluations (and TOR-TILD workflows) with a hybrid method that uses ML interatomic potentials to rapidly sample atomic configurations and applies quasi-harmonic corrections (with targeted anharmonic adjustments in the fluid state) to capture vibrational and electron-vibration entropy contributions.
generation.conditions: The approach is applied at elevated temperatures near melting/fusion (e.g., between 0.7 and 1.1 times the fusion temperature) for elemental and binary systems, and can be extended to multicomponent systems (HEAs) where traditional methods become prohibitively slow.
generation.structural_mediator: The ML-derived potential captures local atomic interactions accurately while the quasi-harmonic approximation mediates the vibrational free energy for ordered solid phases; minimal MD sampling is used for the fluid state to correct anharmonic contributions.
generation.mechanism: ML potentials, trained on DFT data, rapidly generate energetically meaningful configurations and forces with near-DFT accuracy. When combined with a quasi-harmonic approximation to obtain vibrational free energies (and supplemented by limited anharmonic corrections for the melt), the method retains key entropy contributions while dramatically reducing simulation times compared to full ab initio MD or TOR-TILD routines.
generation.predicted_outcome: The hybrid method should yield free energy differences and derived fusion temperature predictions with an accuracy close to ab initio MD benchmarks while offering an order-of-magnitude reduction in computational cost relative to explicit MD workflows, and significantly faster performance than TOR-TILD on multicomponent systems.
generation.baseline: Current explicit ab initio molecular dynamics workflows and TOR-TILD methods, which provide high-fidelity but computationally expensive free energy evaluations.
generation.boundary: Valid for systems where DFT data for training is accessible and the quasi-harmonic approximation remains reasonable (e.g., solids that do not experience extreme anharmonicity) and temperatures up to near-fusion; uncertainties increase for systems with very strong electron-vibration coupling or for melts with pronounced anharmonicity.
generation.uncertainty: The hybrid method may underestimate anharmonic effects in the fluid phase and could introduce systematic errors in electronic entropy contributions. The degree of speedup and fidelity preservation may vary depending on the system complexity and quality of ML potential training data.

falsification_experiment.design: Select a set of benchmark elemental and binary systems with known high-temperature solid-liquid free energy differences (and derived fusion temperatures) from full ab initio MD studies. Compute the free energies using the hybrid ML+quasi-harmonic approach over the same temperature range and compare the predicted fusion temperatures and free energy differences against the established ab initio MD or TOR-TILD results.
measurements: Total free energy differences between solid and liquid phases as a function of temperature
Melting/fusion temperature determined from the free energy crossover
Computational time required to reach convergence
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the hybrid method yields free energy differences or melting point predictions that deviate by more than an acceptable error margin (e.g., >10 meV/atom free energy difference or >50 K in melting temperature) relative to ab initio MD benchmarks, or if computational cost savings are not at least one order of magnitude over TOR-TILD for multicomponent systems, then the hypothesis is falsified.

In this section, we discuss the results of the development of the interatomic-potential model used to enable the application of MD simulations of dislocation properties in bcc MoNbTaW. We employ the general framework of machine-learning (ML)-based approaches, which have emerged recently as a systematic framework to develop potentials with accuracies near that of the underlying DFT calculations for elemental and multicomponent systems,. Here, using training data reported previously for elemental, binary, ternary, and quaternary systems in Nb–Ta–Mo–W, we developed a potential for the MoNbTaW RHEA based on the moment tensor potential (MTP) formalism, which has been found to feature an excellent balance between accuracy and computational cost. The flowchart for constructing the MTP is shown in Fig. 1a with the methodological details provided in “Methods”. The basic materials property predictions of the MTP model are provided in Supplementary Table 1. reading.lever: Integrate ML interatomic potentials with quasi-harmonic corrections to approximate free energies cost-effectively.
reading.why: This hybrid approach, proven for dislocation studies in related systems, promises similar fidelity at a fraction of ab initio MD cost while capturing key entropic effects.
